\section*{Limitations}
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
\item \textbf{Model coverage.} Primary experiments use Qwen3-32B with cross-model validation on Llama-3.1-8B, 70B-Instruct (FP8), and Gemini 2.5 Flash (API). Dimension~1 (count-associated decline) has been validated on a proprietary model (Gemini 2.5 Flash, $\rho = -0.900$, $p = 0.037$; Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix_cross_model_gemini}); Dimension~2 (confusability-associated type substitution) has been verified only on open-weight models. Dimension~2 was not robustly detectable on NER at 8B scale, likely due to floor effects.

\item \textbf{Modest pairwise effect size.} Pairwise SCS explains 1.3--1.7\% of type confusion variance; entity frequency, prompt position, mention ambiguity, and type definition quality likely account for the remainder.

\item \textbf{Factorial interaction tests.} Within-dataset count $\times$ BCS interaction on Few-NERD did not reach significance ($p = 0.50$; Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix_factorial}). A FewRel factorial with TOST equivalence testing is consistent with bounded interaction under the primary linear specification ($p_{\text{TOST}} = 0.003$ at $\pm 3$\,pp, interaction = 0.47\,pp); however, the logit-scale TOST is inconclusive ($p = 0.209$). At $n = 69$, the logit-scale test achieves 80\% power only at margins $\geq 0.25$ logit ($\approx$6\,pp), exceeding our $\pm 3$\,pp margin (0.156 logit); we therefore cannot rule out a meaningful interaction on the logit scale. Cross-pool slope consistency ($p = 0.60$) corroborates stable rather than amplifying sensitivity. For the NER batch-level null ($r \approx 0$, $n = 450$), the minimum detectable effect at 80\% power is $r = 0.13$, well above the observed value; the null is thus not attributable to insufficient power.

\item \textbf{Single-seed evaluation.} BCS-controlled experiments use a single seed with greedy decoding; given the residual SD of 0.88\,pp under greedy decoding (Appendix~\ref{app:variance-decomposition}), the typical 2.2\,pp gap is robust, though its precise magnitude may vary across seeds.

\item \textbf{Decomposition and metric scope.} RE batch composition is tested on FewRel only; NER merge alternatives remain unexplored. Appendix Table~\ref{tab:scs_baselines} shows that SCS outperforms string overlap (Levenshtein), ontological distance (WordNet Wu-Palmer), and same-parent indicators on pairwise confusion prediction ($\rho = 0.218$ vs.\ next-best 0.097 on FewRel; $\rho = 0.166$ vs.\ 0.152 on Few-NERD). String overlap fails entirely on RE ($\rho = 0.016$, n.s.), where semantically similar relations have dissimilar surface forms. Embedding similarity captures semantic proximity that simpler measures miss, though the margin is smaller on NER where hierarchical naming conventions provide partial signal. Label entropy or ontological depth may capture complementary dimensions. For Few-NERD, SCS is computed from the extraction model's own embeddings (Qwen3), which creates a shared-representation dependency. MiniLM cross-check yields a conservative but directionally consistent estimate ($r = 0.172$ vs $r = 0.138$; confusion matrix correlation 0.894); the effect is thus unlikely an artifact of shared representations.

\item \textbf{NER evaluation metric.} Our exact-match NER evaluation conflates boundary errors (partial span overlap) with type errors (correct span, wrong label). Relaxed matching may yield different confusability effect sizes, as boundary ambiguity may correlate with schema complexity independently of type similarity.

\item \textbf{RE format specificity.} RE's clean dimension separation may reflect its closed-set classification format. FewRel combines training and validation splits for 80 types and characterizes classification accuracy rather than end-to-end extraction.

\item \textbf{Causal mechanism.} The study establishes correlational evidence with controlled stratification; mechanistic analysis at the attention or logit level is needed to confirm the causal pathway. The controlled stratification provides evidence consistent with a directional relationship but does not establish interventional causality. A post-hoc schema label renaming experiment was inconclusive due to label unfamiliarity confounds; confusability may require addressing at the schema design stage rather than through surface-level relabeling.

\item \textbf{Task format dependency.} BCS batch-level prediction is demonstrated only under RE's forced-choice classification format, where all errors are type substitutions. An unconstrained decoding ablation ($n = 25$) confirms this: removing the enum constraint eliminates the BCS--accuracy correlation ($\rho = -0.14$, $p = 0.49$), establishing that the batch-level confusability signal is specific to forced-choice RE rather than a general IE phenomenon.

\item \textbf{Data contamination.} FewRel (2018) may appear in pretraining corpora. However, train-origin relations show numerically lower accuracy than val-origin ($-8.8$\,pp, $p=0.06$, n.s.), opposite to the contamination hypothesis. Moreover, the monotonic count-dependent degradation curve (85.7\%$\to$50.4\%) cannot be explained by uniform contamination, which would elevate all conditions equally. BCS slope consistency across independent and within-pool conditions (permutation $p = 0.60$) provides a robustness check that is difficult to reconcile with non-uniform contamination, which would differentially affect specific type subsets. DocRED (2019) provides a lower-contamination-risk replication with consistent BCS--accuracy slopes ($R^2 = 0.53$). Adding train-origin ratio as a covariate leaves the BCS partial effect unchanged ($p = 0.245$ for origin; Appendix~\ref{app:split-origin}).
\end{enumerate}

典型审稿意见："The paper presents extensive statistical analysis but lacks concrete examples. Show specific instances where high-SCS type pairs lead to substitution errors. A confusion matrix heatmap or top-10 most confused pairs table would make the abstract correlational findings more tangible."
